subject: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates

messages.author: 7a32b1066f8fa3ad
messages.subject: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates
parts:
I am a PhD student conducting a research in the field of economics. I have used Lavaan to design a SEM model with 5 latent variables (D, G, W, C and M) and 9 observable variables. The fit of the model looks well as shown below (RMSEA = 0.051, CFI = 0.994 and TLI = 0.991). 


Also I have run the model with OpenMx, and the output of this software tells me that the model is locally identified at solution but not locally identified at the start values. 


Moreover I have used the lavpredict function to obtain the predicted values of the latent variables.   


I'll be grateful if you can provide me with the following feedback: 


1) Do you think that the fact that the model is locally identified at solution but not locally identified at the start values is an issue with regard to the reliability of factor score estimates? 


2)  Does Lavaan provide explicit information on the identification of the model, both at solution and start values? 


3) As far as I know the lavpredict function can be ran using two alternative methods: "regression" and "Bartlett" . Could you give me further details on which regression method is used? (I.e.Thompson-Thurstone or other...)  


4) What is the status of Lavaan as regards the supply of information on the quality of predicted factor scores (standard errors, …)? 


Thanks. 


Next is my model definition and results output from Lavaan: 

 

Model148 <- ' 

W =~ GDPCAP + TECHINBAND  

G =~ INSPROPRO + PRIMEDUC  

C =~ ETHICBEHAV + IRREPAY  

M =~ TECHAVLAT + TECHFIRMABS + FOMASIZE 

D =~ W + G + C + M' 

fit148 <- sem(Model148, data = Datvarpap8) 

summary(fit148, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, rsq = TRUE)

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates
parts:
Jesus--
     "Identified at start values" does not mean very much if start values are arbitrary--like getting the weather forecast for some arbitrary location. If you chose meaningful start values and found the model not identified, that could possibly mean something.
     The larger problem that you have is with factor indeterminacy (Guttman 1955). The common factor model has an indeterminacy built into it, so that the factors are partly arbitrary in their values. Each factor is partly a weighted function of the data (this is what you get from the regression method or Bartlett's method or any of the 4 or 5 other methods) and partly a function of an arbitrary vector. Especially when there are few observed variables per common factor, the degree of indeterminacy--the weight given to the arbitrary component--will be quite large. The indeterminacy means that different sets of factor scores can be equally consistent with the same factor model, BUT those different sets of scores need not be highly correlated (or even positively correlated) with each other--because they are largely arbitrary. Particularly given that you do not have many observed variables given the number of common factors, you should give up the notion of finding values for the common factors. You are asking more of the analytical technique than it can provide.
--Ed Rigdon
Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

parts:
Edward,

 

      Thanks for your clarification and for the reference by Guttman 1955.

      In fact I have a set of over 50 observable variables available that are rather correlated to each other as a whole. Therefore, it is not surprising that the model is not identified at the start values. In spite of that, there are strong theoretical bases to sort the observable variables into the 4 factor scores (G, W, C, M) of the model. Before making the variable selection I have followed both PCA and EFA analyses and could even set alternative models with a similar fit quality and up to 3 observable variables per factor score. 

      Obviously I understand from your reasoning that if the model is identified at the solution, it makes sense to estimate the dependent factor score (D).

      With regard to the estimates of the independent factor scores (G, W, C, M) I understand your skepticism. However, since I have been able to get regression score estimates and both the results and the allocation of observable variables to factor scores make sense from a theoretical standpoint, do you think the model could be tenable somehow?

Jesús Matos

messages.subject: Re: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates
parts:
Jesus

The problem that I see in your model is that is globally identified (meaning that has positive df), but most constructs are not locally identified. You want to have both, local identification means that each construct its identified by itself, if you were to run a model with only that construct it would be identified to be estimated.

A way to identifed locaaly tour model would be something like this, note that I am adding std.lv=T to set the identification by standardizing the latent variables, without it the default is to set by fixing a factor loading to 1.
This code is identifing the constructs with 2 indicators by fixing the 2 factor loading to the same value, this way each construct is just identify

Model148 <- ' 

W =~ a*GDPCAP + a*TECHINBAND  

G =~ b*INSPROPRO + b*PRIMEDUC  

C =~ c*ETHICBEHAV + c*IRREPAY

M =~ TECHAVLAT + TECHFIRMABS + FOMASIZE 

D =~ W + G + C + M'
fit148 <- sem(Model148, data = Datvarpap8, std.lv=T)
summary(fit148, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, rsq = TRUE)

     "Identified at start values" does not mean very much if start values are arbitrary--like getting the weather forecast for some arbitrary location. If you chose meaningful start values and found the model not identified, that could possibly mean something.
     The larger problem that you have is with factor indeterminacy (Guttman 1955). The common factor model has an indeterminacy built into it, so that the factors are partly arbitrary in their values. Each factor is partly a weighted function of the data (this is what you get from the regression method or Bartlett's method or any of the 4 or 5 other methods) and partly a function of an arbitrary vector. Especially when there are few observed variables per common factor, the degree of indeterminacy--the weight given to the arbitrary component--will be quite large. The indeterminacy means that different sets of factor scores can be equally consistent with the same factor model, BUT those different sets of scores need not be highly correlated (or even positively correlated) with each other--because they are largely arbitrary. Particularly given that you do not have many observed variables given the number of common factors, you should give up the notion of finding values for the common factors. You are asking more of the analytical technique than it can provide.
--Ed Rigdon
Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates
parts:
Jesus,

I think "local identification" is a heuristic.  A model is either globally identified or not, and if it is not, then you look for clues about which part of the model might not be "locally" identified so you can solve the problem.  Identification can depend on aspects of your data, not just counting the number of free parameters and observed sample moments.  A 2-indicator CFA by itself is not identified without the constraints such as the ones you used (or, for example, fixing both factor loadings to 1 and estimating the common factor variance and both unique factor variances).  But when you have multiple 2-indicator constructs in a model, it can be identified (i.e., a unique solution can be found), as long as the constructs correlate.  Steiger illustrates this in the first section of this article:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//1082-989X.7.2.210

I didn't see any evidence of empirical underidentification in your original model, but the model with equal factor loadings fits poorly and yields estimates at the border ("Heywood cases").  So I would recommend trusting the results from the less constrained model in your original post.  But I also agree with Ed that factor score indeterminacy is an important limitation to using factor scores.  If you were planning to use the factor scores in a subsequent model, you would probably be better off just incorporating that model into this model to estimate those parameters (assuming the model is not so large that your small sample size becomes a limiting factor).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts:
Terrence,

Thanks for your comments and reference recommendation.

I will not use the factor score values to build a subsequent model. Just to set in context, I am using observations over 142 countries to study a broad economic pattern which is described by factor score D.  In turn, factor scores W, G, C and M are also latent constructs collecting specific attributes that conform D. My main purpose is to obtain a rank of countries according to the estimated measure of factor score (attribute) D. It might be interesting for my research to analyze the values, subsequently the country rankings, according to factor scores (attributes) W, G, C and M and the correlation (interaction) among them.

I agree with the assessment made in the forum regarding factor indeterminacy. Would that be reasons that offset - acceptably -  the indeterminacy hindrance?

Jesus,

I think "local identification" is a heuristic.  A model is either globally identified or not, and if it is not, then you look for clues about which part of the model might not be "locally" identified so you can solve the problem.  Identification can depend on aspects of your data, not just counting the number of free parameters and observed sample moments.  A 2-indicator CFA by itself is not identified without the constraints such as the ones you used (or, for example, fixing both factor loadings to 1 and estimating the common factor variance and both unique factor variances).  But when you have multiple 2-indicator constructs in a model, it can be identified (i.e., a unique solution can be found), as long as the constructs correlate.  Steiger illustrates this in the first section of this article:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//1082-989X.7.2.210

I didn't see any evidence of empirical underidentification in your original model, but the model with equal factor loadings fits poorly and yields estimates at the border ("Heywood cases").  So I would recommend trusting the results from the less constrained model in your original post.  But I also agree with Ed that factor score indeterminacy is an important limitation to using factor scores.  If you were planning to use the factor scores in a subsequent model, you would probably be better off just incorporating that model into this model to estimate those parameters (assuming the model is not so large that your small sample size becomes a limiting factor).
